title: POC - BYO network patterns and DNS handoff
content:
Purpose:
This note collects pragmatic BYO (bring-your-own) network patterns for customer POCs where the customer wants Redwood Private/Dedicated inside their VPC or on-prem fabric. Focus: simple, testable connectivity approaches, DNS handoff patterns, ingress/egress tradeoffs, and a short validation checklist for a POC-run.

Context and constraints typical for these POCs:
- Customer controls their VPCs and routing (BYO).
- Must avoid permanent IP ownership assumptions — treat POC as ephemeral.
- Minimum change to customer infra preferred (security teams often block new peering/transit projects).
- Need TLS and mTLS where possible, and clear audit trail for egress.
- Some customers require all egress through their proxy (corporate firewall) or via constrained NAT.

Assumptions:
- Redwood control plane can operate across the public internet or private link depending on customer preference.
- POC focuses on inference planes (model hosting) connecting to customer on-prem data or APIs.
- Customer has an account with cloud provider (AWS/GCP/Azure) and can provision endpoints.

Three pragmatic connectivity patterns (fastest -> most integrated):

1) Interface Endpoints + Private DNS (low customer lift)
- Summary: Create provider-managed interface endpoints (ENIs) or cloud provider interface endpoints in customer VPC that point to Redwood ingress endpoints. Use conditional/private DNS to resolve service names to the interface endpoints.
- When to use: Customer cannot/do not want transit/peering but can accept inbound interface endpoints and security group rules. Works well for short-term POCs.
- Pros: Low networking change, minimal routing impact, easy to revoke.
- Cons: Requires customer to accept inbound connectivity; may not match enterprise egress/inspection requirements.
- Key steps: Provision interface endpoint, update Private Hosted Zone with A/AAAA records, create SG allowing port 443 from customer subnets, verify TLS with customer certs if required.

2) Private Service Connect / PrivateLink + Route controls (medium integration)
- Summary: Use cloud provider private link equivalents (GCP Private Service Connect, AWS PrivateLink, Azure Private Link) to expose Redwood services as private endpoints in customer VPC. Combine with private DNS for hostnames.
- When to use: Customer requires private connectivity without full peering or transit. Useful when traffic must never traverse public internet.
- Pros: Strong isolation, no cross-account routing required, good for regulated workloads.
- Cons: Requires provider-side setup (service attachment), potential cost per endpoint.
- Key steps: Create service attachment on Redwood side, customer creates endpoint in VPC, populate private DNS, test TCP/TLS handshake and application-level auth.

3) Transit / Shared VPC / Peering (deep integration)
- Summary: Full VPC peering or Transit Gateway / VPC Network Peering to allow direct routing between customer VPCs and Redwood-managed compute VPCs. Combine with centralized NAT or firewall for controlled egress.
- When to use: Enterprise POCs expecting to scale into a production relationship and need full routing, high throughput, and centralized security controls.
- Pros: High performance, native routing, central logging.
- Cons: Higher operational/approval burden, requires CIDR planning, potential route table complexity.
- Key steps: Agree on CIDR non-overlap, set up peering/transit attachment, exchange route tables, test cross-AZ throughput, ensure SG/NACL hygiene.

DNS handoff patterns and guidance:
- Split-horizon DNS is the safest default: customer private zone overrides public resolution for service hostnames used by Redwood endpoints.
- Options:
  - Private hosted zone owned by customer that maps redwood-service.<customer-domain> -> interface endpoint IPs.
  - Conditional forwarding from customer DNS to a Redwood-managed resolver for certain subdomains (useful for hybrid scenarios).
  - Short-lived CNAME handoff: during POC, create a CNAME from a customer-managed hostname to a Redwood-managed ephemeral domain; revert after POC.
- Avoid: changing global public DNS during an ephemeral POC unless both parties accept risk.
- TLS: prefer SAN entries including the customer hostname; use certs from customer PKI or Let’s Encrypt if approved.

Ingress/egress considerations:
- Ingress options: interface endpoints/private link or allowing customer-initiated outbound connections to Redwood (webhook style). Decide based on customer security team preference.
- Egress control patterns:
  - Customer-managed NAT/proxy: preferred by strict customers — all outbound hits customer proxy for inspection. Redwood should support proxy auth/headers.
  - Redwood-managed egress via customer's firewall IP allowlist: simplest for POC; customer whitelists Redwood egress IPs.
  - Brokered egress via TLS tunnel (mutual TLS) back to customer collector: useful when customer won’t allow direct inbound endpoints.
- Logging and audits: push flow logs (VPC flow logs, ELB logs) to customer-owned bucket or SIEM where feasible. For transit patterns, mirror subnets to IDS/IPS if required.

Service endpoints and authentication:
- Use mTLS for node-to-node control plane calls where feasible.
- Token-based auth for inference APIs; rotate tokens per POC.
- Short-lived client certs: issue ephemeral client certs for customer teams to validate end-to-end TLS.

Security controls checklist (POC-minimum):
- SGs: least privilege — only necessary ports (443, 8443) and CIDR ranges.
- NACLs: align with SGs but remember stateless enforcement.
- IAM/service accounts: scope to least privilege for any infra provisioning scripts.
- Logging: enable VPC flow logs and export to customer bucket or shared project.
- Secrets: never place RW DB creds in plain text; use customer KMS where required.

Lightweight validation checklist for a POC run (run these in order):
1) DNS resolution from a customer-hosted test VM to redwood-service.<customer-domain> returns interface endpoint IP(s).
2) TLS handshake completes and server cert SAN matches expected hostname.
3) Token auth handshake: POST /v1/auth -> 200 (token issued).
4) Small inference request roundtrip latency < target (baseline test).
5) Confirm egress path: capture via tcpdump and match to expected NAT/proxy IP.
6) Flow logs show allowed return traffic and no unexpected drops.
7) Cancel/tear down endpoint: ensure removal leaves no public records.

Operational notes and POC playbook tips:
- Keep CIDRs small for POC: /28 or /27 endpoints reduce risk and routing complexity.
- Automate teardown: provide customer with a script or CloudFormation/Terraform to remove endpoints and DNS records when POC ends.
- Offer a “read-only” logging hookup: easiest win for security teams is to show flows to their SIEM rather than ask for full control plane network access.
- When in doubt, start with interface endpoints or PrivateLink — they unblock legal/security faster.

Open decision log for this POC:
- DNS ownership: customer will own private hosted zone for poc.redwood.<customer-domain> (agreed 2025-09-10).
- Egress model: use customer-managed proxy for outbound calls to external APIs (customer policy).
- Certificate model: issue short-lived SAN certs via customer PKI (pending approval from security).

Remaining questions / blockers:
- Does customer require IDS/IPS traffic mirroring for the endpoint subnet?
- Are there hard constraints on specific port ranges for inference traffic besides 443?
- Will customer accept redwood egress IP whitelisting as temporary fallback?

References and snippets:
- Quick test curl: curl -v --resolve "redwood-svc.poc.customer:443:10.10.0.12" https://redwood-svc.poc.customer/health
- Example Terraform: provide a minimal module to create an interface endpoint and private DNS record; keep in repo github.com/redwood-inference/private-deployments/poc-byo-templates

Next steps:
- Iterate this doc with customer network/infra lead and security (schedule 30-min network handshake).
- Draft Terraform module and teardown script; share in the POC repo.
- Validate mTLS flow with SE infra team and produce checklist for call.

Notes to self / rough TODOs (quick):
- Draft PrivateLink pricing note for customer (cost per endpoint).
- Add GCP-specific Private Service Connect example (customer uses GCP).
- Confirm whether customer will allow cross-account role for Redwood to create endpoints (some customers prefer self-provisioning).

-- End of POC notes --
